subject: zoology
question_text: Write eight salient features of the class Amphibia.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.39, SAQ 36). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. BOOK ERROR: the book prints 'Hyla (free frog)'. Hyla is the TREE frog; 'free' is a misprint for 'tree', and the card writes tree frog.

steps.label: Habitat and body
steps.margin_note: Eighteen features are printed and eight are asked. Take two to five per mark, grouped.
lines: 1) Amphibians are the first tetrapods, the
first animals with four limbs.
2) They live both on land and in water.
3) The body is divided into head, trunk and
tail. The tail may be present or absent.
4) The skin is moist, glandular and without
scales.
5) The limbs are pentadactyl: five digits on
each limb.
steps.why: The moist naked skin is the key to the whole class, because it is what lets an amphibian breathe through the skin and what keeps it tied to water.
common_mistakes: Writing that amphibians have scales. Their skin is naked; scales appear first in reptiles.
Saying all amphibians have a tail. A frog loses its tail as an adult; a salamander keeps it.
steps.memory_tip: Amphi means both: both land and water, and a skin that has to stay wet for it.

steps.label: Skeleton
steps.margin_note: Three skeletal features. The sternum line is the one examiners look for.
lines: 6) The skull is dicondylic: it has two
occipital condyles.
7) The vertebrae are procoelous, amphicoelous
or opisthocoelous.
8) The sternum appeared for the first time in
amphibia.
steps.why: The sternum is a new bone that appears with limbs, because a four limbed animal needs a chest to brace the front limbs against, so this feature belongs with the tetrapod line.
common_mistakes: Writing that the skull is monocondylic. That is the bird and reptile condition; amphibians have two condyles.
Saying the sternum is absent. It appears for the FIRST time in this class.
steps.memory_tip: First tetrapods, so the first sternum: limbs and a chest bone arrive together.

steps.label: Respiration, heart, excretion
steps.margin_note: Group breathing, heart and excretion into one mark. Name all three routes of respiration.
lines: 9) Respiration is of three kinds: pulmonary
(by lungs), cutaneous (by the moist skin) and
bucco-pharyngeal (by the lining of the mouth).
10) The heart is three chambered, with two
auricles and one ventricle.
11) The sinus venosus and the conus arteriosus
are both present.
12) The kidneys are mesonephric.
13) Amphibians are ureotelic; they give out
urea.
steps.why: Three ways of breathing follow from the moist skin of the first feature, so this block is the working out of a fact already written.
common_mistakes: Naming only lungs. Skin and mouth lining are two separate marked routes.
Writing that amphibians are ammonotelic. They are ureotelic and give out urea.
steps.memory_tip: Three ways to breathe: lungs, skin, mouth. All three need the skin to stay moist.

steps.label: Sense organs and reproduction
steps.margin_note: Finish with the examples. Four named genera round off the eight features.

lines.text: Moist skin, no scales, 3 chambered heart

lines: 14) The meninges are two: piamater and
duramater.
15) The middle ear has a columella auris, a
small rod that carries sound from the tympanum
to the internal ear.
16) Lacrimal and harderian glands are present
in the eye and keep it moist.
17) Sexes are separate. Fertilisation is
external and the larva is a tadpole.
18) Examples: Bufo (toad), Rana (frog), Hyla
(tree frog), Rhacophorus (flying frog).
steps.why: External fertilisation and a tadpole larva are the last tie to water, so the class that began on land still has to return to water to breed.
common_mistakes: Writing that amphibians have three meninges. They have TWO; three are found in mammals.
Saying fertilisation is internal. In frogs and toads it is external, in water.
steps.memory_tip: Two meninges, one ear bone, external fertilisation: the class is only half way onto land.

insider_note: Eight features are asked but eighteen are printed, so choose the eight that are hardest to guess — dicondylic skull, first sternum, three routes of respiration, two meninges — and number them.
